messages.author: 970bb92277d806ae
messages.subject: The right way of fixing parameters for vectors of different lenghts
parts:
Hi, everyone,

I have this model with parameters theta, referring to terms (T) of parties (P). Not necessarily, the number of terms is equal for every party.
I mean, whereas party X1 refers to the years 2000, 2001, 2002, party X1 refers to 2002,2003.

"
parameters {
  vector[2] alpha_beta[R];        // position and discrim of Rollcall r
  vector[P] theta[T];            // position in term t of party p
}
"

I want to find a way of fixing some of those thetas. In this case, for example, theta[1,1] would be equal to -2, and theta[10,1], to 3.

How would I do that?

In a unidimensional case, I would do something like:

"parameters {
  vector[P-2] theta;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[P] new_theta;
  for (i in 2:9)
    new_theta[i] <- theta[i];
  for (i in 11:P)
    new_theta[i] <- theta[i];
  new_theta[1] <- -2;
  new_theta[10] <- 3;
}
"

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] The right way of fixing parameters for vectors of different lenghts
parts:
Exactly the same way, so I'm not sure what you're
asking. Is it an issue with raggedness or setting fixed
values?

I'd also recommend

new_theta[1] <- -2;
new_theta[2:9] <- theta[1:8];
new_theta[10] <- 3;
new_theta[11:P] <- theta[9:(P - 2)];

instead of the loop version you had that will go out
of bounds for theta.

- Bob

Bob,

sorry. I don't think my question has been clear enough.

What I been asking is is there a straightforward way of fixing values for parameters without having to part and transform them?

I tried another strategy that is easier but turned the code too slow: attributing a normal prior with a low variance. For example, x ~ normal(3, 0.00001).

I highly agree that it is okay to transform parameters in order to fixing them. The problem is: when we are doing this with vectors, the code looks messy to me.

Is there another way to do that?

Thanks for your help

Thanks, Bob. I'll try to describe my problem , but I'm convinced now to use low variance priors ( N(3, 0.0000001) ), even if it sounds like a workaround.

First off, we have a bayesian IRT model with parties (46) and terms (25 years). The first problem is, in the first term, we have only 10 parties, and some of them cease to exist before the last term. In order to solve identifiability problems, I want to fix initial priors for 6 parties: 3 parties which begin in the first term, and 3 parties, which begin in the fourth term.  I know I can model this in Stan with:
"
"parameters {
vector[P] theta[T];            // position in term t of party p

...
}
model {
   theta[1] ~ normal(-3, 0.000001);
   theta[2] ~ normal(-2, 0.000001);
   theta[10] ~ normal(2, 0.000001);
   theta[25] ~ normal(3, 0.000001);
   ...

It's worth mentioning again, we don't have the same number of parties per term. In term 1, there are 10 parties, in term 5, as an example, there could be 15 parties.

Okay, I'd like to find a way of fixing those values instead of defining priors with low variance. In cases of standard IRT models, it's easy to do that.
On the contrary, in cases of dynamic models, it's been hard and I've got lots of "Rejecting initial value:" messages.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: The right way of fixing parameters for vectors of different lenghts
parts:
I'm afraid I still don't understand where the question
is in all of this.

Are you only using normal(3, 0.0000001) because you don't like
how the transformed parameters look?

If you have rejecting initial value messages, that means you
are supplying initializations that do not have positive
density. You need to make sure the inits for every parameter
match the constraint on the parameter. Our automatic inits
do that. If you have problems with auto inits, it's usually due
to missing constraints in the parameter declarations.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] The right way of fixing parameters for vectors of different lenghts
parts: Hi, you really don't want to do this:
theta[1] ~ normal(-3, 0.000001);

If you really want to specify something like that, do it like this:
theta[1] = theta_1 + 0.000001*epsilon[1];
epsilon[1] ~ normal(0,1);
and specify theta_1 as data (giving it the value -3).

This should work better.  You can get all sorts of problems working with a distribution like normal(-3, 0.000001);
A

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: The right way of fixing parameters for vectors of different lenghts
parts:
It's better for three reasons. First, if you use default starting values, Stan will pick values between -1 and 1 for the parameters. So you want them to be roughly on unit scale. Second, it helps when looking at output to be able to see the posterior uncertainties; this will be easier for epsilon than for theta which would have to be displayed to 6 significant digits. Third, Stan's optimization or HMC sampler works best when the parameters are on roughly a common scale.
A

That's my whole model. Could someone check it?

stan_code <- '

data {
int<lower=0> N;                 // number of votes
int<lower=0> P;                 // number of different parties
int<lower=0> R;                 // number of different rollcalls
int<lower=0> T;                 // number of different terms

int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N]; // vote (yea = 1, nay = 0)
int<lower=0> p[N]; // parties
int<lower=0> r[N]; // rollcals
int<lower=0> t[N]; // terms


vector[2] b0;                   // prior mean for pos and discrim
cov_matrix[2] B0;               // prior covar for pos and discrim

}
parameters {
  vector[2] alpha_beta[R];        // position and discrim of Rollcall r

vector[P-3] first_theta;            // position in term t of party p (first theta)
  vector[P] next_theta[T-1];            // position in term t of party p (next theta)
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[P] theta[T];
  theta[1,1] = -2.0; // PT
  theta[1,2] = 3.0;
  theta[1,3] = first_theta[1]*1;
  theta[1,4] = 2.0;
  theta[1,5:13] = first_theta[2:10]*1;
  theta[1,14:P] = first_theta[11:(P-3)]*1;
  for (i in 2:T) theta[i, P] = next_theta[(i-1),P]*.2;

}
model {
  for (n in 1:N) {
    y[n] ~  bernoulli_logit(alpha_beta[r[n], 1] + alpha_beta[r[n], 2] * theta[t[n], p[n]]);
  }
  alpha_beta ~ multi_normal(b0, B0);
 
  first_theta ~ normal(0, 1);
  next_theta[1,] ~ normal(0, 1);
  for (i in 2:(T-1))
    next_theta[i] ~ normal(next_theta[i - 1], 1);
}

'
